name: António de Oliveira Salazar
period: Later Estado Novo government, 1950–1968; earlier institutions used to interpret continuing rule
description: Portuguese ruler assessed through later corporatist government, economic opening, colonial policy and the negotiated relationship between the state and Catholic Church.

religion.reason: Adult Catholic identification is established separately from his insistence that clergy remain outside state politics.

sources.title: António de Oliveira Salazar — biography and positions

axes.brief: Controlled elections and restricted opposition placed effective authority in the executive.
axes.counterEvidence: Formal assemblies and corporative consultation existed without competitive alternation.

axes.brief: Political police and censorship prioritised state order over dissent.
axes.counterEvidence: Nominal constitutional rights and nonpolitical private life prevent describing every restriction as identical to total mobilisation.

axes.brief: Portuguese imperial unity and national moral education privileged a shared official identity.
axes.counterEvidence: Lusotropical claims and legal assimilation complicate simple biological-race exclusion without erasing colonial inequality.

qualifications.15: The statement specifically includes several distinct ways of life within national identity; it does not ask whether a common national identity should exist.

axes.brief: Sovereignty and administrative screening favour managed migration.
axes.counterEvidence: Wartime refugees and colonial mobility are different from modern asylum caps; nationality was not simply a racial test.

qualifications.5: The statement permits permanent refugee settlement regardless of skills or cultural compatibility. The answer concerns this unconditional clause, separately from selected humanitarian admissions.

axes.brief: Colonial wars and military readiness took precedence over yielding claimed national territory.
axes.counterEvidence: Second World War neutrality and diplomacy qualify a general appetite for intervention.

axes.brief: Colonial sovereignty and resistance to external pressure constrain international jurisdiction.
axes.counterEvidence: NATO, EFTA and multilateral economic membership demonstrate pragmatic cooperation.

axes.brief: Private companies and property remained prominent within corporatist regulation and public infrastructure.
axes.counterEvidence: State economic direction does not mean every productive asset was publicly owned.

axes.brief: EFTA and outward investment increased openness while strategic and colonial economic preferences continued.
axes.counterEvidence: Earlier protection and licensing persisted unevenly; free trade was selective rather than unlimited.

axes.brief: Private production operated within licensing, corporative bargaining and national development priorities.
axes.counterEvidence: Fiscal restraint and market expansion qualify comprehensive command planning.

axes.brief: Property, fiscal discipline and corporative welfare favour a limited safety net over equalisation.
axes.counterEvidence: Catholic social duties and later public provision prevent treating assistance as categorically illegitimate.

axes.brief: Catholic education and marriage privileges coexist with legal separation and executive primacy.
axes.counterEvidence: Voluntary school opt-outs and civil marriage remained; the Church did not receive an unrestricted political veto.

axes.brief: Traditional family and public moral order formed the social programme.
axes.counterEvidence: Pragmatic economic adaptation is independent of sexual and family-policy change.

axes.brief: Development plans supported useful industrialisation while cautious social policy limited transformative change.
axes.counterEvidence: Economic conservatism is not opposition to all technology; modern genetic questions require analogy.

qualifications.13: Controlled embryo-enhancement trials are still a reproductive intervention. Catholic moral commitments make rejection more likely even where practical industrial modernisation is supported.

axes.brief: The unitary executive subordinated local and colonial institutions to national policy.
axes.counterEvidence: Administrative districts and corporative councils did not possess federal constitutional independence.

axes.brief: Education and Catholic socialisation shape behaviour alongside traditional assumptions about sex and temperament.
axes.counterEvidence: Imperial hierarchy does not prove a genetic theory for each group difference; racial doctrine differed from Nazi biology.
